q: The barrier potential of a silicon PN junction at room temperature is about:
explanation: Silicon ≈ 0.7 V, germanium ≈ 0.3 V. (1.1 eV is the band-gap energy of silicon, not the barrier voltage.)
why: That is silicon’s band gap in eV.
Typical of a red LED forward drop.

q: An N-type semiconductor is obtained by doping silicon with:
explanation: Pentavalent donors (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) give free electrons. Trivalent acceptors (boron, gallium, indium, aluminium) give P-type.

q: Majority carriers in a P-type semiconductor are:
explanation: Acceptor atoms create holes, which are the majority carriers; electrons are minority carriers.
why: Ions are fixed in the lattice and do not conduct.

q: A PN junction diode is forward biased when:
options: P side is connected to the negative terminal
P side is connected to the positive terminal
Both sides are at the same potential
N side is connected to positive
explanation: Positive to the anode (P) reduces barrier width and allows large current once the cut-in voltage is exceeded.

q: A Zener diode is normally used as a voltage regulator in:
explanation: In reverse breakdown the voltage across a Zener stays nearly constant over a wide current range.
why: Forward bias behaves like an ordinary diode.

q: Zener breakdown (as opposed to avalanche breakdown) occurs in:
options: Lightly doped junctions at high voltage
Heavily doped junctions at low voltage (below about 5 V)
explanation: Heavy doping gives a very thin depletion layer and an intense field that pulls electrons from covalent bonds (tunnelling). Above ~6 V avalanche multiplication dominates.

q: A Zener regulator: input 20 V, V_{Z} = 12 V, series resistor 200 Ω, load 1 kΩ. Zener current is:
In a BJT, the emitter current is:
explanation: KCL on the transistor: I_{E} = I_{B} + I_{C}.

q: A transistor has α = 0.98. Its β is:
A BJT with β = 100 has base current 20 µA (active region). Collector current is:
The common-emitter configuration is most widely used for amplifiers because it gives:
options: Both current and voltage gain (highest power gain)
explanation: CE gives good current and voltage gain with a 180° phase reversal. CC (emitter follower) has A_{v} ≈ 1; CB has low input impedance.

q: An emitter follower (common-collector) is mainly used as a:
explanation: High input impedance, low output impedance and voltage gain ≈ 1 make it ideal for buffering.

q: Compared with a BJT, a FET:
options: Is voltage-controlled with very high input impedance
Is current-controlled with low input impedance
explanation: FETs are unipolar, voltage-controlled devices with very high input impedance; BJTs are bipolar and current-controlled.

q: An ideal operational amplifier has:
options: Zero input impedance and infinite output impedance
Infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance
explanation: Ideal op-amp: A_{OL} = ∞, Z_{in} = ∞, Z_{out} = 0, infinite bandwidth and CMRR, zero offset.
why: That is a voltage follower configuration.

q: An inverting op-amp amplifier has R_{f} = 100 kΩ and R_{in} = 10 kΩ. Its voltage gain is:
A non-inverting amplifier uses R_{f} = 100 kΩ and R_{1} = 10 kΩ. Its gain is:
In an inverting amplifier with negative feedback, the inverting input is at "virtual ground" because:
options: Very high open-loop gain forces the differential input voltage to almost zero
The input current is very large
It is physically connected to ground
explanation: With A_{OL} → ∞ and finite output, v_{+} − v_{−} → 0; v_{+} is grounded so v_{−} ≈ 0 V, yet draws no current.

q: Which logic gates are called universal gates?
explanation: Any Boolean function can be built using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

q: The decimal equivalent of binary 1011 is:
The binary equivalent of decimal 25 is:
An XOR gate gives a HIGH output when:
explanation: XOR = AB′ + A′B: output is 1 only when inputs differ; used in adders and parity checkers.

q: According to De Morgan's theorem, (A·B)′ equals:
explanation: (AB)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′B′.

q: Minimum number of flip-flops needed for a mod-10 (decade) counter is:
why: Ring counters use 10 but are not minimal.

q: A PMMC (permanent magnet moving coil) instrument can measure:
explanation: Deflecting torque ∝ instantaneous current; with AC the average torque is zero. It has a linear scale and high accuracy. Moving-iron instruments work on both AC and DC.

q: Moving-iron instruments:
options: Work on both AC and DC with a non-uniform scale
Are used only for power measurement
explanation: Torque ∝ I^{2}, so direction is unaffected by current reversal; scale is crowded at the low end.

q: A megger is used to measure:
explanation: A megger applies a high DC test voltage (500 V–5 kV) and reads in megohms. Earth resistance is measured with an earth tester.
why: Kelvin double bridge measures low resistance.

q: Kelvin double bridge is used to measure:
explanation: It eliminates the effect of lead and contact resistances. Wheatstone bridge: medium resistance; megger/loss-of-charge: high resistance.

q: Schering bridge is used to measure:
explanation: Schering bridge measures capacitance and dissipation factor of insulation (cables, bushings) at high voltage.
why: Maxwell, Hay and Anderson bridges measure inductance.

q: Hay's bridge is preferred over Maxwell's bridge for measuring inductance of coils with:
explanation: Maxwell's inductance–capacitance bridge suits medium Q (1–10); Hay's bridge suits high-Q coils.
why: Maxwell's bridge is used for medium Q.

q: Wien bridge is commonly used for:
options: Measuring frequency and in RC oscillators
explanation: Balance depends on frequency (f = 1/(2πRC) for equal arms); the same network sets frequency in Wien-bridge oscillators.

q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge P = 1000 Ω, Q = 100 Ω and S = 47 Ω. Unknown R is:
A meter with internal resistance 100 Ω and full-scale current 1 mA is to read 1 A full scale. Shunt resistance is about:
The same 1 mA, 100 Ω movement is to be used as a 100 V voltmeter. Series multiplier resistance is:
why: That is total resistance including the meter.

q: A voltmeter movement has full-scale current 50 µA. Its sensitivity is:
An ammeter is connected in ___ and should have ___ resistance.
explanation: Series connection measures the circuit current; low resistance avoids altering it. A voltmeter is in parallel with very high resistance.
why: A low-resistance meter in parallel shorts the circuit.
High series resistance would reduce the current.

q: A single-phase induction-type energy meter can be used on:
explanation: It relies on eddy currents induced in an aluminium disc by alternating fluxes of the shunt and series magnets.
why: DC would induce no eddy currents.

q: An energy meter has constant 1200 rev/kWh. A 2 kW load runs for 30 minutes. Number of disc revolutions is:
why: 3 times too large — a typical formula slip.

q: "Creeping" in an induction-type energy meter is:
options: Rotation of the disc at no load
explanation: Over-compensation for friction can make the disc rotate slowly with only the pressure coil energised; two diametrically opposite holes in the disc prevent it.

q: A clamp-on (tong) tester is used to measure:
explanation: Its jaws form a CT core around the conductor (or use a Hall sensor for DC).

q: Lissajous patterns on a CRO are used to determine:
options: Frequency ratio and phase difference of two signals
explanation: Applying signals to X and Y plates gives figures whose shape gives frequency ratio (tangency counts) and phase (ellipse).
why: Voltage is read from the graticule directly.

q: A meter reads 98 V when the true value is 100 V. Percentage error is:
The electrodynamometer instrument is most commonly used as a:
explanation: Fixed current coil and moving pressure coil give torque ∝ VI cos φ; works on AC and DC.

q: Loading effect in voltage measurement is minimised by using a voltmeter of:
explanation: A high-resistance voltmeter draws little current and disturbs the circuit less.
why: MI voltmeters usually have low Ω/V.
